Every radius is positive since h_C(u)≥−R and T_k>R. On expanding the squared radius, its excess over T_k²+2T_k h_C(u)+R² is 2T_k/k+(h_C(u)+1/k)²−R²>0. Thus every original point is interior to every ball, and finiteness gives ambient interior containment. Each ball satisfies its stated supporting inequality; the signed coordinate inequalities give B=√m(R+1).

For a nearest point c to exterior x, the normal v=(x−c)/|x−c| satisfies v·(w−c)≤0 for all w∈C, by the derivative of squared distance along [c,w]. Thus h_C(v)=v·c. Bounding |h_C(u)−h_C(v)| by R|u−v| and |x·(u−v)| by B|u−v| gives exactly the displayed Hausdorff error. The open segment between any two distinct intersection points lies in the interior of each ball, hence in the interior of their finite intersection.

The common ambient bound gives a finite lattice base set, including the single empty-tuple base if n=0. An absent original fiber cannot recur infinitely by compactness and Hausdorff convergence. At a present base, outer containment gives one Hausdorff direction and the same compactness argument gives the other, even for a lower-dimensional original fiber. A relative neighborhood in the ambient slice about each original point gives full continuous dimension of the approximating slice.

Strict convexity of a positive approximating slice follows from the ambient open-segment test. A supporting hyperplane in continuous coordinates intersects that slice in at most one point. For d≥2 this is section-null; for d=1 a support meets a single endpoint of H^0 mass one. For d=0 the measures are counting measures on the eventually equal base set.

At a fixed point of a present base, outer containment gives persistent inclusion and slice convergence gives eventual exclusion outside the original closed slice. With stable absence of other bases, dominated convergence on a finite collection of bounded slices yields M_k→M. Since μ_k−μ is nonnegative, its mass δ_k is the exact supremum of its Borel set values, attained by the whole space. This handles closed halfspace boundaries of positive mixed mass.

For each y the cap infima satisfy 0≤b−a≤δ_k and 0≤a≤M. The difference between b/M_k and a/M is [M(b−a)−aδ_k]/(MM_k), whose numerator is the difference of two numbers in [0,Mδ_k], giving δ_k/M_k with no factor of two.

For a finite Borel measure and any fixed closed cap containing y, outward positive threshold slack eventually contains a sequence converging to y. Continuity from above as slack decreases to zero gives the upper-semicontinuity inequality for that cap, and infimizing gives it for depth. A subsequential limit stays on the closed mixed lattice and lies in C by the Hausdorff bound. Uniform depth error tending to zero and upper semicontinuity preserve the same c at that limit.

overlap.comparison: This assumes a fixed finite base set of positive approximating and limiting fibers with fiberwise Hausdorff convergence, and proves a symmetric-difference depth estimate and moving-mark continuity. It does not supply strictly convex ambient outer bodies, base stability, possible null limiting slices, the exact normalized estimate under containment, or d=0.

Its fixed canonical-lift residual families allow null limit fibers and give depth continuity under simultaneous fiber convergence. The frozen theorem supplies ambient outer approximants and exact mass control for arbitrary convex bodies and includes counting measure.

The upper semicontinuity of raw mixed depth on the sampled set overlaps. The frozen proof establishes upper semicontinuity for arbitrary finite ambient measures and uses it with uniform depth convergence from the explicit approximants.

This assumes section nullity on the original positive fibers to prove strict interpolation. The frozen theorem provides approximants meeting that premise when d≥2 and transfers numerical lower depth bounds, not conclusions about the number of maximizers.

readability: “Each original nonempty integer fiber is full-dimensional in C_k” means that the corresponding fiber of C_k is full-dimensional in its continuous affine slice. The proof explicitly allows the original fiber itself to be lower-dimensional.
